decks.title: The Cholas — Part 1: Sources and Kings
goals: Explain the value of Chola inscriptions, including those on village administration, as sources
Describe the Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur as a source for Chola history
List the major Chola kings in chronological order, including Vijayalaya, Rajaraja I and Rajendra I

slides.heading: The Cholas: sources and kings
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we know about the Cholas, and who ruled.

nodes.label: Sources: inscriptions and the Brihadishwara Temple

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the sources, which are inscriptions and the Brihadishwara Temple, and then the Chola kings in order
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we learn how historians know about the Cholas. We study inscriptions, including those about village government, and the great temple at Thanjavur. Then we meet the Chola kings in order, from Vijayalaya to Rajendra the First.

slides.heading: Three kinds of source

rows: Writing cut into temple walls and stones
Land gifts written on metal sheets
Royal gifts and the family and deeds of a king
A great temple of Shiva at Thanjavur
Royal power, building skill, art and belief

visual.alt: Table of three Chola sources: stone inscriptions, copper-plate grants and the Brihadishwara Temple, with what each helps us learn

slides.narration: Three kinds of source help us. Stone inscriptions are cut into temple walls. Copper plate grants are land gifts written on metal sheets. The Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur is itself a source. Each tells us something different about the Cholas, and each needs to be read with care.

slides.heading: Chola inscriptions
bullets: Record **gifts of land and lamps**, orders, rules and names.
Made at the time, so they are **direct evidence**.
Royal praise may **exaggerate**; compare with other sources.

rows: On temple walls and on stones
Gifts of land and lamps, orders, rules and names
Made at the time, so direct evidence
Royal praise may exaggerate; compare with other sources

visual.alt: Table about Chola inscriptions: found on temple walls and stones, recording gifts, orders, rules and names, valuable as direct evidence, with the care that royal praise may exaggerate

slides.narration: Chola kings and their officials had many inscriptions cut on temple walls and on stones. They record gifts of land and lamps, orders, rules and names. Because they were made at the time, they are direct evidence. But where they praise a king, a historian is careful and compares them with other sources.

slides.heading: Copper-plate grants

rows: Copper-plate grants of the Chola kings
A set kept in the Netherlands, named after its present home
Names, gifts and dates are useful; praise needs care

visual.alt: Table of three named sets of Chola copper-plate grants, the Anbil, Thiruvalangadu and Larger Leiden plates, and how to use them

slides.narration: Chola kings also issued copper plate grants. Three well known sets are the Anbil plates, the Thiruvalangadu plates and the Larger Leiden plates. They are useful for names, gifts and dates. Remember that a grant often praises the king, so read that part with care.

slides.narration: Look back at the sources. Match each name or term with what it is. Think about which one is a set of copper plate grants, and which one is a way of choosing members.

slides.heading: The Uttaramerur inscriptions
bullets: From the reign of **Parantaka I**, about **919 and 921 CE**.
Describe how a village **sabha** chose members and ran committees.

rows: Reign of Parantaka I; about 919 and 921 CE
How a village sabha chose its members and ran committees

visual.alt: Table about the Uttaramerur inscriptions: in Kanchipuram district, from the reign of Parantaka I about 919 and 921 CE, about how a village sabha chose members and ran committees, important as evidence of local self-government

slides.narration: The Uttaramerur inscriptions are found in present day Kanchipuram district. They date from the reign of Parantaka the First, about nine hundred nineteen and nine hundred twenty one of the common era. They describe how a village sabha chose its members and ran its committees, which makes them very important.

slides.heading: Choosing members by lot

nodes.label: The village is divided into wards
Names of eligible persons go on palm leaves
Leaves are put in a pot
One leaf is drawn by lot for each ward

visual.alt: Flow of the kudavolai method: the village is divided into wards, names of eligible persons are written on palm leaves, the leaves are put in a pot, and one is drawn by lot for each ward
visual.caption: Choosing sabha members by lot (kudavolai).

slides.narration: The village was divided into wards. The names of eligible persons were written on palm leaves and put in a pot. One leaf was then drawn by lot for each ward. This method is called kudavolai. It gave every eligible person a fair chance.

slides.heading: Qualifications, disqualifications, committees
bullets: **Qualifications**: some land and a house, a suitable age, learning.
**Disqualifications**: for example, no accounts of an earlier post.

rows: Owning some land and a house; an age within a set range; knowledge of the Vedas or of administration
For example, failing to give accounts of an earlier post, or serious wrongdoing
For tanks, gardens, justice and other village work

visual.alt: Table of the Uttaramerur rules as commonly taught: qualifications such as land, a house, age and learning; disqualifications such as failing to give accounts; and committees called variyams for tanks, gardens and justice

slides.narration: As commonly taught, a candidate needed some land and a house, an age within a range, and knowledge of the Vedas or of administration. Some people were disqualified, for example those who had not given accounts of an earlier post. The sabha also had committees, called variyams, for tanks, gardens and justice.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using an inscription as a source
slides.body_md: Name it, say what it records, say what it shows, add a care.

rows: Inscriptions of the reign of Parantaka I
Rules for choosing a village sabha
It shows one village, so not every village was alike

visual.alt: Table of four steps for using an inscription as a source, applied to the Uttaramerur inscriptions: name the source, say what it records, say what it shows and add one care

slides.narration: Here is a method for any source question. First name the source. Second say what it records. Third say what it shows. Fourth add one care. For the Uttaramerur inscriptions, they record rules for a village sabha, they show organised local self government, and the care is that they show one village, so not every village was alike.

slides.heading: The Brihadishwara Temple
bullets: Built by **Rajaraja I**; completed about **1010 CE**.

rows: Vimana of about 66 metres, a massive Nandi, a large linga, painted murals, inscriptions

visual.alt: Table about the Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur: built by Rajaraja I, completed about 1010 CE, dedicated to Shiva, with a vimana of about 66 metres, a massive Nandi, a large linga, painted murals and inscriptions

slides.narration: Rajaraja the First built the Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur, and it was completed about one thousand ten of the common era. It is dedicated to Shiva. Its towering vimana is about sixty six metres high. It also has a massive Nandi, a large linga, painted murals and inscriptions on its walls.

slides.heading: The temple as a source

rows: Gifts to the temple, events and names
The power and resources of the king
Art, dress and belief of the age
Listed in 1987 as part of the Great Living Chola Temples; extended in 2004

visual.alt: Table of what a historian can learn from the Brihadishwara Temple: inscriptions show gifts, its size shows royal power, murals show art and belief, and it is part of the World Heritage Site Great Living Chola Temples, listed 1987 and extended 2004

slides.narration: The temple tells us a great deal. Its inscriptions record gifts. Its size and planning show the power and resources of the king. Its murals and sculpture show art and belief. It is part of the World Heritage Site called the Great Living Chola Temples, listed in nineteen eighty seven and extended in two thousand four.

slides.heading: Great Living Chola Temples

visual.alt: Table of the three temples of the World Heritage Site Great Living Chola Temples: the Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur, the temple at Gangaikondacholapuram and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram, added in 2004

slides.narration: The World Heritage Site has three temples. The Brihadishwara Temple is at Thanjavur. A second temple is at Gangaikondacholapuram, linked with Rajendra the First. The third is the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram. The last two were added when the site was extended in two thousand four.

visual.caption: The Chola kings (approximate dates).

slides.narration: This time line is drawn roughly to scale. Vijayalaya took Thanjavur about eight hundred fifty. Aditya the First followed him. Parantaka the First ruled from about nine hundred seven to nine hundred fifty five. Rajaraja the First ruled to about one thousand fourteen, and Rajendra the First to about one thousand forty four. Always say about with these dates.

slides.heading: Vijayalaya, Aditya I and Parantaka I
bullets: **Vijayalaya**, about **850 CE**: took **Thanjavur**, founded the later Chola line.
**Parantaka I**, about **907 to 955 CE**: the Uttaramerur inscriptions come from his reign.

rows: Took Thanjavur and founded the later (imperial) Chola line
Successor of Vijayalaya; strengthened the young kingdom
Uttaramerur inscriptions of his reign, about 919 and 921 CE

visual.alt: Table of three early kings: Vijayalaya about 850 CE who took Thanjavur, Aditya I before 907 CE, and Parantaka I about 907 to 955 CE in whose reign the Uttaramerur inscriptions were made

slides.narration: Vijayalaya took Thanjavur about eight hundred fifty and founded the later, or imperial, Chola line. Aditya the First succeeded him. Parantaka the First ruled from about nine hundred seven to nine hundred fifty five, and the Uttaramerur inscriptions on village government belong to his reign.

slides.heading: Rajaraja I

rows: Extended Chola power in the south
Sri Lanka and the Maldives; a strong navy
The Brihadishwara Temple, completed about 1010 CE

visual.alt: Table about Rajaraja I, about 985 to 1014 CE: extended Chola power in the south, reached Sri Lanka and the Maldives with a strong navy, and built the Brihadishwara Temple

slides.narration: Rajaraja the First ruled from about nine hundred eighty five to one thousand fourteen. He extended Chola power in the south, reached Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and had a strong navy. He also built the Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur.

slides.heading: Rajendra I

rows: Naval expedition to Srivijaya in South-East Asia, about 1025 CE

visual.alt: Table about Rajendra I, about 1014 to 1044 CE: the expedition to the Ganga and the title Gangaikondachola, the new capital Gangaikondacholapuram, and a naval expedition to Srivijaya about 1025 CE

slides.narration: Rajendra the First ruled from about one thousand fourteen to one thousand forty four. He led an expedition to the Ganga and took the title Gangaikondachola. He founded a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram. About one thousand twenty five he sent a naval expedition to Srivijaya in South East Asia.

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: sources, the Uttaramerur inscriptions, and the Chola kings in order

slides.narration: To sum up. Our sources are inscriptions, copper plate grants and the Brihadishwara Temple, all read with care. The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe a village sabha in the reign of Parantaka the First. The kings in order are Vijayalaya, Aditya the First, Parantaka the First, Rajaraja the First and Rajendra the First.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Say **about** with every date; books differ.
For a source, give **what it records**, **what it shows** and **one care**.
Write the Uttaramerur rules **in your own words**.
Keep the **order** of the kings clear.
slides.narration: Some exam habits. Add the word about to every date. For a source, say what it records, what it shows and one care. Write the Uttaramerur rules in your own words. Spell the long names carefully. Keep the order of the kings clear, from Vijayalaya to Rajendra the First.

sections.body_md:
- **Stone inscriptions** were cut on temple walls and stones. They record gifts of land and lamps, orders, rules and names, and being made at the time they are direct evidence.
- **Copper-plate grants** record land gifts. Well-known sets are the **Anbil**, **Thiruvalangadu** and **Larger Leiden** plates.
- Royal praise in a grant may exaggerate, so historians compare it with other sources.

sections.heading: 2. The Uttaramerur inscriptions
sections.body_md:
- **Where and when:** present-day Kanchipuram district; reign of **Parantaka I**, about **919 and 921 CE**.
- **Choosing members:** the village was divided into wards. Names of eligible persons were written on palm leaves, put in a pot and drawn by lot, a method called **kudavolai**.
- **Qualifications** (as commonly taught): owning some land and a house, an age within a set range, and knowledge of the Vedas or of administration.
- **Disqualifications:** for example, failing to give accounts of an earlier post, or serious wrongdoing.
- **Committees (variyams)** looked after tanks, gardens, justice and other work.

sections.heading: 3. The Brihadishwara Temple as a source
sections.body_md:
- Built by **Rajaraja I** at **Thanjavur** and completed about **1010 CE**; dedicated to **Shiva**.
- Features: a towering **vimana** of about **66 metres**, a massive **Nandi**, a large **linga**, painted **murals** and **inscriptions** on its walls.
- It shows the power and resources of the king, and records gifts.
- Part of the World Heritage Site **Great Living Chola Temples** (listed **1987**, extended **2004** to add Gangaikondacholapuram and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram).

sections.heading: 4. Chola kings in order
sections.body_md:
- **Vijayalaya** (about 850 CE): took Thanjavur and founded the later (imperial) Chola line.
- **Aditya I:** his successor, before 907 CE.
- **Parantaka I** (about 907 to 955): the Uttaramerur inscriptions belong to his reign.
- **Rajaraja I** (about 985 to 1014): power in the south, Sri Lanka and the Maldives, a strong navy, the Brihadishwara Temple.
- **Rajendra I** (about 1014 to 1044): expedition to the Ganga, the title **Gangaikondachola**, the new capital **Gangaikondacholapuram**, and a naval expedition to **Srivijaya** (South-East Asia) about 1025.
- **Kulottunga I** (about 1070 to 1120) is sometimes added.
- Dates are approximate and books vary; say **about**.

key_terms.definition_md: A title meaning the Chola who took the Ganga.
A maritime kingdom of South-East Asia.

sections.heading: 5. Administration and village self-government
sections.body_md:
- The **king** was helped by ministers and officials.
- The kingdom was divided into **mandalams** (provinces, often under princes or viceroys), then **valanadus or nadus** (districts), then **villages**.
- Local assemblies: the **ur** (ordinary villages, landholders), the **sabha** (brahmadeya villages) and the **nagaram** (merchants in trade centres).
- **Committees** managed tanks, gardens, temples and justice.
- **Land revenue** was the main income; land was surveyed.

key_terms.definition_md: A district; also called a nadu.
An assembly of merchants in a trade centre.

sections.heading: 6. Temple architecture
sections.body_md:
- Chola temples follow the **Dravida** style.
- Parts: a **vimana** (pyramidal tower over the sanctum, very tall at Thanjavur), a **gopuram** (gateway tower, larger in later temples), **mandapas** (pillared halls) and an **enclosure wall**.
- Do not mix up the vimana and the gopuram.

The inner chamber of a temple.

sections.heading: 7. Bronze sculpture
sections.body_md:
- Bronze images were cast by the **lost-wax (cire perdue)** method: wax model, clay coating, heating so the wax melts out, pouring molten metal, breaking the mould, finishing.
- The **Nataraja** shows Shiva as Lord of Dance in a ring of flames, a symbol of the cosmic cycle of creation and destruction.
- Chola bronzes are admired for **balance, grace and fine detail**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about.
- Mixing up the vimana (over the sanctum) and the gopuram (gateway).
- Mixing up the ur, the sabha and the nagaram.
- Putting Rajendra I before Rajaraja I.
- Listing the lost-wax steps in the wrong order.
- Treating royal praise in a grant as proved fact.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a reason, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A student of the imagined Class IX at Gyan Jyoti School is asked to name one set of Chola copper-plate grants for a wall chart. Which entry is correct?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Anbil plates. The Anbil plates, with the Thiruvalangadu and Larger Leiden plates, are examples of Chola copper-plate grants. The other three belong to the Gupta and Mauryan periods.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Vellaru Heritage Centre, a card says that a king's copper-plate grant of a village begins with long praise of his family and victories. How should a student use this grant as a source?

options.text_md: Accept every claim of victory as proved, because metal does not change
Ignore the grant, because praise makes it useless
Use it only to learn the colour of the metal
Treat the gift of the village as useful evidence but read the praise with care and compare it with other sources

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Treat the gift of the village as useful evidence but read the praise with care and compare it with other sources. A grant is a valuable record of gifts, places and rulers, but praise of a king is meant to please, so it is checked against other evidence. It is neither proof of every claim nor useless.

questions.stem_md: A page of the imagined Chola Trail booklet says the Uttaramerur inscriptions, from the reign of Parantaka I, are found in the present-day district of:
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Kanchipuram. Uttaramerur lies in present-day Kanchipuram district. The other districts are in the same part of the country but are not where these inscriptions are found.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined notes of a village record keeper named Kanagan, each eligible name was written on a palm leaf, the leaves were placed in a pot and one was drawn for each ward. What was this method of choosing members called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Kudavolai. Drawing names written on palm leaves from a pot is the kudavolai system described in the Uttaramerur inscriptions. A variyam is a committee, a nagaram a merchants' assembly and a brahmadeya a village granted to Brahmanas.

questions.stem_md: Ilango of the imagined village of Mullaikudi owns a house and a plot of land, is within the age range and knows the work of administration. Under rules like those at Uttaramerur, which further fact would still keep him out of the sabha?

options.text_md: He owns two plots of land instead of one
He lives in a house with a tiled roof
He earlier held a committee post and never submitted its accounts
He learned administration from his grandfather

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He earlier held a committee post and never submitted its accounts. Rules of this kind barred people who had failed to give accounts of an earlier office, as commonly taught. Owning more land, the roof of a house or the source of one's learning are not disqualifications.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Thanjavur Visitors' Guide says that the vimana of the Brihadishwara Temple rises to about how many metres?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** About 66 metres. The vimana is commonly given as about 66 metres high. The other figures are far too small or too large for the tower.

questions.stem_md: During an imagined debate, a student says, "The Brihadishwara Temple is only a place of worship, so it tells us nothing about the Chola state." Which reply is the best?

options.text_md: The student is right, because buildings never help historians
It tells us only the weather of the region
It tells us only about the Gupta age
The inscriptions on its walls and its size and planning also show the king's power, gifts and resources

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The inscriptions on its walls and its size and planning also show the king's power, gifts and resources. Inscriptions record gifts and events, and a building on this scale reflects royal power and resources, so it is a source for politics as well as religion. The other replies deny this or are unrelated.

questions.stem_md: A quiz card in the imagined Chola Heritage Club asks which three temples make up the World Heritage Site called the Great Living Chola Temples. Which answer is correct?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Thanjavur, Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram. The site includes the Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur, the temple at Gangaikondacholapuram and the Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram. The other sets mix in monuments of other places and periods.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chola inscriptions are valuable sources for historians.

**Reason (R):** They record gifts, village rules and the names of rulers and places, often on the walls of temples, so they give direct evidence of the period.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: the direct records of gifts, rules and rulers are what make them valuable.

questions.stem_md: True or false? According to the Uttaramerur inscriptions, a village sabha could choose its members by drawing lots.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Names of eligible persons were put in a pot and drawn by lot, which is called the kudavolai method.

questions.stem_md: The Uttaramerur inscriptions date from the reign of ___, about 919 and 921 CE.
questions.solution_md: They belong to the reign of Parantaka I.

questions.stem_md: Match each source of Chola history with what it is.

match_right.text_md: Records of how a village sabha was run
Choosing members by drawing names from a pot
A temple of Shiva at Thanjavur, completed about 1010 CE

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The Anbil plates are copper-plate grants, the Uttaramerur inscriptions describe a village sabha, the Brihadishwara Temple was completed about 1010 CE, and kudavolai is the lot system.

questions.stem_md: Why are stone inscriptions and copper-plate grants valuable sources for the Chola period? Give two points.
questions.solution_md: Direct records; local rules and gifts.

answer.model_answer_md: They are **direct records made at the time**, so they give names of rulers, places and gifts. Many also describe **local rules**, such as those of village assemblies, which books written much later rarely mention.

marking_scheme.step: Direct records of rulers, places and gifts

questions.stem_md: A student in the imagined history club says that every claim in a royal grant must be exactly true. Give two reasons why a historian would be careful.
questions.solution_md: Praise may exaggerate; compare with other evidence.

answer.model_answer_md: Such grants often begin with **praise of the king**, which may exaggerate his deeds. A historian therefore **compares the grant with other evidence**, such as other inscriptions, before accepting a claim.

marking_scheme.step: Grants open with royal praise that may exaggerate

questions.stem_md: State two features of the Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur that make it an important source.
questions.solution_md: Any two: vimana, Nandi, murals, inscriptions.

answer.model_answer_md: It has a **tall vimana of about 66 metres**, a massive **Nandi**, a large linga and painted **murals**. Its walls also carry **inscriptions**, and it was built by **Rajaraja I**.

questions.stem_md: Describe, in three points, how the Uttaramerur inscriptions show that a Chola village sabha followed fixed rules.
questions.solution_md: Lot system; qualifications; disqualifications and committees.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The village was divided into **wards**, and members were picked by **drawing lots** (kudavolai) from names written on palm leaves.
2. Candidates needed **qualifications**, such as owning land and a house, a suitable age and knowledge of the Vedas or administration.
3. There were **disqualifications** and **committees (variyams)** for tanks, gardens and justice.

questions.stem_md: Give three facts about the Brihadishwara Temple: its builder, its date and its place in world heritage.
questions.solution_md: Builder; date; World Heritage listing.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It was built by **Rajaraja I** and dedicated to **Shiva**.
2. It was completed about **1010 CE** at **Thanjavur**.
3. It is part of the World Heritage Site called the **Great Living Chola Temples**, listed in **1987** and extended in **2004** to include Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram.

marking_scheme.step: Rajaraja I as builder, dedicated to Shiva

questions.stem_md: An imagined guide at Thanjavur tells a group, "Everything on these walls is a document." Give three kinds of information a historian can draw from the temple and its walls.
questions.solution_md: Gifts; power and wealth; art and beliefs.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **inscriptions** record **gifts of land and lamps** made to the temple.
2. The **size and design** of the building show the **power and wealth** of the king who built it.
3. The **murals and sculpture** show the **art and beliefs** of the time.

questions.stem_md: A family tree in the imagined Chola Gallery begins with the ruler who took Thanjavur about 850 CE and founded the later (imperial) Chola line. Whose name goes at the top?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Vijayalaya. Vijayalaya took Thanjavur about 850 CE and began the line. Rajaraja I, Rajendra I and Kulottunga I ruled much later.

questions.stem_md: A card in a school quiz says: "This king led an expedition to the Ganga, took the title Gangaikondachola and founded a new capital." Which king is meant?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rajendra I. Rajendra I took the title Gangaikondachola and founded Gangaikondacholapuram. Rajaraja I built the Thanjavur temple, and Parantaka I and Aditya I ruled earlier.

questions.stem_md: A museum guide in the imagined town of Vennaiyur says, "This king added the Maldives and parts of Sri Lanka to his power, built a strong navy, and raised a great temple at Thanjavur." Which king is described?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rajaraja I. These achievements belong to Rajaraja I. Rajendra I is known for the Ganga expedition and the Srivijaya voyage, while Vijayalaya and Aditya I belong to the early line.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined project on sea trade, a student writes that a Chola fleet sailed to Srivijaya in South-East Asia about 1025 CE. Which king sent it?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rajendra I. The naval expedition to Srivijaya is linked with Rajendra I. The others are not associated with this voyage.

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum label gives the reign of Rajaraja I as about 985 to 1014 CE and of Rajendra I as about 1014 to 1044 CE. About how many years do the two reigns cover together?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** About 59 years. Counting from 985 to 1044 gives about 59 years. Twenty-nine and thirty are the lengths of single reigns, and 95 comes from a slip in subtracting.

questions.stem_md: Four students of the imagined Arivu Academy arrange Chola rulers on a wall. Which arrangement is correct, earliest first?

options.text_md: Parantaka I, Vijayalaya, Rajendra I, Rajaraja I
Rajaraja I, Vijayalaya, Parantaka I, Rajendra I
Vijayalaya, Parantaka I, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I
Vijayalaya, Rajendra I, Parantaka I, Rajaraja I

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Vijayalaya, Parantaka I, Rajaraja I, Rajendra I. The order is Vijayalaya (about 850), Parantaka I (about 907 to 955), Rajaraja I (about 985 to 1014) and Rajendra I (about 1014 to 1044). The others place at least one pair the wrong way round.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined seminar must pick the strongest evidence for the claim that the Cholas were a naval power. Which is best?

options.text_md: The height of the vimana at Thanjavur
The Chola hold on the Maldives and the sea expedition to Srivijaya about 1025 CE
The lot system in village assemblies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Chola hold on the Maldives and the sea expedition to Srivijaya about 1025 CE. Taking island territory and sending a fleet across the sea need a navy. A tall tower, a village election method and bronze casting show other strengths, not sea power.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Srivijaya expedition shows the strength of the Chola navy under Rajendra I.

**Reason (R):** It was a voyage across the sea to South-East Asia, about 1025 CE.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: crossing the sea to South-East Asia could be done only with a strong fleet.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Kulottunga I (about 1070 to 1120) ruled before Rajaraja I.
questions.solution_md: **False.** False. Kulottunga I ruled after Rajaraja I (about 985 to 1014) and Rajendra I.

questions.stem_md: After his expedition to the Ganga, Rajendra I took the title ___.
questions.solution_md: He took the title Gangaikondachola.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these Chola kings in chronological order, earliest first.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Vijayalaya, Aditya I, Parantaka I, Rajaraja I and Rajendra I.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State two achievements of Rajaraja I.
questions.solution_md: Conquests and naval power; the temple.

answer.model_answer_md: He extended Chola power in the **south**, including **Sri Lanka** and the **Maldives**, using a strong **navy**. He also built the **Brihadishwara Temple** at Thanjavur, completed about 1010 CE.

marking_scheme.step: Conquests in the south, Sri Lanka or the Maldives

questions.stem_md: State two achievements of Rajendra I.
questions.solution_md: Ganga expedition and capital; Srivijaya.

answer.model_answer_md: He led an **expedition to the Ganga** and took the title **Gangaikondachola**, founding **Gangaikondacholapuram** as a new capital. He also sent a **naval expedition to Srivijaya** about 1025 CE.

marking_scheme.step: Ganga expedition, title or new capital

questions.stem_md: Give one important fact each about Parantaka I, Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, with their approximate reigns.
questions.solution_md: One fact for each king.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Parantaka I** (about 907 to 955): the **Uttaramerur inscriptions** on village government come from his reign.
2. **Rajaraja I** (about 985 to 1014): he built the **Brihadishwara Temple** and extended Chola power by land and sea.
3. **Rajendra I** (about 1014 to 1044): he took the title **Gangaikondachola** and sent a fleet to **Srivijaya**.

marking_scheme.step: Parantaka I with reign and fact
Rajaraja I with reign and fact
Rajendra I with reign and fact

questions.stem_md: An imagined student draws a timeline that puts Rajendra I before Rajaraja I and gives the Srivijaya expedition to Vijayalaya. Correct the two mistakes.
questions.solution_md: Correct order; correct king for Srivijaya.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Rajaraja I** (about 985 to 1014) ruled **before** Rajendra I (about 1014 to 1044), who was his successor.
2. The **Srivijaya expedition**, about 1025 CE, was a **naval** venture of **Rajendra I**.
3. **Vijayalaya**, about 850 CE, belongs at the **start** of the timeline.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Chola Gallery chart, the largest divisions of the kingdom, often placed under princes or viceroys, are labelled with which term?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Mandalam. A mandalam was a province. A gopuram is a temple gateway, a variyam a committee and a nagaram an assembly of merchants.

questions.stem_md: A record keeper's imagined chart shows three levels: a mandalam, then a group of villages under one name, then the single village. What is the middle level called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Valanadu or nadu. The division between mandalam and village was the valanadu or nadu, a district. A brahmadeya is a type of village, and mandapa and vimana are parts of temples.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined ordinary village of Pallikudi, the landholders meet under a tree to settle the use of a common pasture. Which body are they forming?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The ur. The ur was the assembly of an ordinary village, for landholders. The sabha belonged to brahmadeya villages, the nagaram to merchants in trade centres, and a variyam was a committee.

questions.stem_md: The imagined village of Chaturvedimangalam was granted to a group of Brahmanas and its affairs are run by their assembly. What is this assembly called?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The sabha. The assembly of a brahmadeya village was the sabha. The ur belonged to ordinary villages, the nagaram to merchants, and a mandalam is a province.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined trade centre of Vennaiyur, cloth sellers, oil merchants and grain dealers meet to decide matters of the market. Which Chola body is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The nagaram. The nagaram was the assembly of merchants in a trade centre. The ur and sabha were village assemblies, and a valanadu was a district.

questions.stem_md: An imagined officer of the Chola treasury, Madhavan, measures fields before fixing what each farmer owes. What main source of income does his work serve?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Land revenue. Land revenue was the main income, and surveying the land helped fix it. The other options are minor or not sources of regular state income.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined seminar says that written rules on qualifications, drawing of lots and committees at Uttaramerur show something about Chola villages. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: Some villages had organised local self-government with rules for choosing and checking members
Villages had no say in any matter
Every village in the kingdom was run in exactly the same way
The king chose every village member directly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Some villages had organised local self-government with rules for choosing and checking members. Fixed rules for selection and committees point to organised local self-government. They do not show that all villages were alike, and the king did not choose each member.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sabha was an assembly of merchants in trade centres.

**Reason (R):** The nagaram was the Chola assembly of merchants in trade centres.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: the sabha was the assembly of brahmadeya villages. R is true: the merchants' body was the nagaram.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Uttaramerur inscriptions are cited as evidence of organised self-government in a Chola village.

**Reason (R):** They set out how members were chosen, with qualifications, disqualifications and committees.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: the detailed rules are what show organised self-government.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Land revenue was the main income of the Chola state, and land was surveyed.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Land revenue was the chief source of income, and surveys helped to fix it.

questions.stem_md: Match each Chola administrative term with its meaning.

questions.stem_md:
Inscriptions are among the best sources for the Chola period.

(i) Name two kinds of inscriptions, with one example of each. **[3]**
(ii) Explain how the Uttaramerur inscriptions show the way a village sabha chose its members. **[3]**
(iii) Explain the value of such inscriptions as sources, and one care a historian must take. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Two kinds with examples; the lot system; value and caution.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Chola kings issued **stone inscriptions**, often cut on temple walls, and **copper-plate grants**. Examples of the grants are the **Anbil plates**, and the Thiruvalangadu or Larger Leiden plates.

(ii) The Uttaramerur inscriptions, of **Parantaka I** (about 919 and 921 CE), say the village was split into wards. Names of eligible persons were written on **palm leaves**, put in a pot and **drawn by lot** (kudavolai).

(iii) They are **direct records** of gifts, rules and rulers, so they show how villages were run. Because royal grants open with praise, they must be **compared with other evidence**.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Direct records of gifts, rules and rulers
(iii) Caution: praise, compare with other evidence

questions.stem_md:
The Brihadishwara Temple at Thanjavur is both a monument and a source of history.

(i) Who built it, when was it completed and to whom is it dedicated? **[3]**
(ii) Describe its main features. **[3]**
(iii) Explain how it helps us to learn about the Cholas, and state its place in world heritage. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Builder, date and dedication; features; value as a source and heritage status.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The temple at **Thanjavur** was built by the king **Rajaraja I** and completed about **1010 CE**. It is dedicated to the god **Shiva**, and it is the best-known monument of the Chola kings.

(ii) A towering **vimana** of about **66 metres** rises above the sanctum. Inside and around it are a massive **Nandi**, a large **linga**, painted **murals** on the walls and long **inscriptions** cut into the stone.

(iii) The inscriptions record **gifts** made to the temple, and the scale of the building points to the **power and wealth** of the king who raised it. In this way a monument of worship also serves as a source for politics and the economy. It belongs to the World Heritage Site **Great Living Chola Temples**, listed in **1987** and extended in **2004** to include the temples at Gangaikondacholapuram and Darasuram.

marking_scheme.step: (iii) Inscriptions and power of the king

questions.stem_md:
The later Chola kings built a powerful state.

(i) List Vijayalaya, Aditya I, Parantaka I, Rajaraja I and Rajendra I in chronological order, with approximate dates where known. **[3]**

(iii) Describe the achievements of Rajendra I. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Order of kings; Rajaraja I; Rajendra I.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The order is **Vijayalaya** (about 850 CE), who took Thanjavur, then **Aditya I**, **Parantaka I** (about 907 to 955), **Rajaraja I** (about 985 to 1014) and **Rajendra I** (about 1014 to 1044). Dates are approximate and books differ a little.

(ii) Rajaraja I won lands in the **south** and in **Sri Lanka**, took the **Maldives** and kept a strong **navy** that made Chola power felt across the sea. He also built the great **Brihadishwara Temple** at Thanjavur, completed about 1010 CE.

(iii) Rajendra I led an expedition to the **Ganga** and took the title **Gangaikondachola**. He founded a new capital, **Gangaikondacholapuram**, and about **1025 CE** he sent a **naval expedition** to **Srivijaya** in South-East Asia, which shows the reach of the Chola fleet.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Five kings in the correct order

questions.stem_md:
The Cholas governed through several levels.

(i) Describe the position of the king and his officials. **[3]**
(ii) Name and describe the divisions of the kingdom. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the three kinds of local assembly and the main source of revenue. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: King and officials; divisions; assemblies and revenue.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) At the head of the state stood the **king**. He was helped by **ministers** and many **officials** who carried out his orders and watched over the work of government in the kingdom.

(ii) The kingdom was divided into **mandalams**, which were provinces, often placed under **princes or viceroys**. Each mandalam held **valanadus or nadus**, which were districts, and each district was made up of many **villages**.

(iii) Local affairs were handled by assemblies. The **ur** served ordinary villages, the **sabha** served **brahmadeya** villages granted to Brahmanas, and the **nagaram** served **merchants** in trade centres. **Land revenue** was the main income of the state, and land was **surveyed** to fix what was due from each holding.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Mandalam, often under princes or viceroys

questions.stem_md:
A student of the imagined Class IX of Tamarai School says: "Chola villages governed themselves."

(i) Name the assemblies through which villages and merchants managed their affairs. **[3]**
(ii) Describe two ways in which the Uttaramerur rules show organised self-government. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate the statement: how far is it fair? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Assemblies; two Uttaramerur features; a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Ordinary villages had the **ur**, an assembly of landholders. Villages granted to Brahmanas, called brahmadeya villages, had the **sabha**. Merchants in trade centres had the **nagaram**, which looked after matters of the market.

(ii) The Uttaramerur inscriptions show that members were picked by **lot** from names on palm leaves, and only those who met the **qualifications** and avoided the **disqualifications** could be listed. The sabha also worked through **committees (variyams)** for tanks, gardens and justice, which shows division of work.

(iii) The statement is **partly fair**. Local bodies had real duties and written rules, so villages did manage many of their own affairs. Yet they worked inside a kingdom headed by the **king**, whose officials and **land revenue** system reached every village, so the self-government was real but not complete.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Lot system with qualifications and disqualifications
(iii) Partly fair, with evidence of local rules
(iii) Limits set by the king and revenue system

questions.stem_md:
Chola temples are remembered for their architecture.

(i) Name the four main parts of a Chola temple in the Dravida style. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the vimana and the gopuram, and how the gopuram changed in later temples. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the Brihadishwara Temple as an example of Chola architecture. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Four parts; vimana and gopuram; Brihadishwara as an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A Chola temple in the Dravida style had four main parts: the **vimana**, the **gopuram**, the **mandapas** and the **enclosure wall** that surrounded the whole temple.

(ii) The **vimana** is a pyramidal tower that rises in storeys above the sanctum. The **gopuram** is the tower over the gateway. In the **later Chola temples** the gopurams became **larger**, so that they came to stand out more than before.

(iii) At **Thanjavur** the Brihadishwara Temple has a vimana of about **66 metres**, which dominates the whole complex. It also has a massive **Nandi**, pillared **mandapas**, painted **murals** and **inscriptions**, and it forms part of the **Great Living Chola Temples**, a World Heritage Site.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined bronze workshop of Murugan makes images in the Chola tradition.

(i) Describe the lost-wax method in its main steps. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the Nataraja and what it is thought to symbolise. **[3]**
(iii) Explain why Chola bronzes are admired. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Lost-wax steps; Nataraja; reasons for admiration.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) First a **wax model** of the image is made, and it is coated with **clay** to form a mould. Next the mould is **heated** so that the wax melts and runs out, and **molten metal** is poured into the empty space. When the metal has set, the **mould is broken** and the image is cleaned and finished.

(ii) The **Nataraja** is an image of **Shiva as Lord of Dance**. The figure dances inside a **ring of flames**, which is commonly read as a symbol of the **cosmic cycle of creation and destruction**.

(iii) Chola bronzes are admired for their **balance**, since the figures seem poised in movement, and for their **grace** of line and expression. They also show **fine detail** in ornaments and features, which the wax model could hold and the metal copied closely.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Lord of Dance in a ring of flames
